annotations.description: In a 4-player Commander game, choosing to go first means you draw fewer cards (no draw on your first turn) and become the first visible threat. With a hand that has no 1-drop or 2-drop creature (only lands, Blackblade Reforged, Military Intelligence, and expensive spells like Notorious Throng and Soul Manipulation), there's little benefit to going first. The hand wants to set up with lands and hold up interaction, which benefits more from drawing extra cards and acting later.
annotations.actionTaken: Chose themselves (Gem25F Analyst) to go first.
annotations.betterLine: Choose a different player to go first, allowing yourself to draw on your first turn and gather more information before committing to plays. Going later in multiplayer with a reactive/slow hand is generally preferable.

annotations.description: Mossfire Valley requires {1} plus tapping to produce mana, so playing it as your only land on turn 1 means you have zero available mana. Forest would give {G} immediately. While there's nothing castable in hand for 1 mana, having mana available is strictly better, and both sequencings produce the same mana on turn 2.
annotations.actionTaken: Played Mossfire Valley as the turn 1 land drop
annotations.betterLine: Play Forest turn 1 (gives {G} available), then Mossfire Valley turn 2 for the same turn 2 mana output but with turn 1 mana access

annotations.description: Playing Swamp is redundant with Vivid Marsh's black mana production. The hand is heavily white-demanding (Hour of Reckoning, Teneb, Karador all need white) and they have no white source yet without spending a Vivid Marsh charge counter.
annotations.actionTaken: Played Swamp, giving redundant black mana alongside Vivid Marsh
annotations.betterLine: Play Plains to diversify mana and have access to white mana without spending Vivid Marsh charge counters, since black is already covered by Vivid Marsh

annotations.description: Playing Orzhov Basilica on turn 3 instead of Plains means bouncing a land back to hand, resulting in only 2 mana available this turn (and the Basilica enters tapped). Playing Plains would give 3 mana available immediately (Plains + Vivid Marsh + Swamp), allowing a turn 3 play like Acorn Catapult. With the Basilica, the bounced land needs to be replayed next turn, effectively setting back mana development by a turn. The Basilica does provide mana fixing and virtual card advantage long-term, but playing Plains first and Basilica later (when there are more lands to bounce without losing tempo) would be better sequencing. Playing Plains now gives 3 mana for Acorn Catapult, then Basilica next turn bouncing a basic still yields 4 mana on turn 4.
annotations.actionTaken: Played Orzhov Basilica, which enters tapped and bounces a land back to hand, leaving only 2 mana sources (one tapped).
annotations.betterLine: Play Plains to have 3 untapped mana available, enabling a turn 3 Acorn Catapult. Play Orzhov Basilica on a later turn when the tempo loss of bouncing a land is less impactful.

annotations.description: Karador, Ghost Chieftain gets cheaper to cast for each creature card in the graveyard, so discarding it loses access to a potentially powerful commander-cost-reduction creature. However, with only 2 lands in play and a hand full of expensive cards, Gem3F ESPN needed to keep lands and more castable cards. The real question is whether discarding Cobra Trap (which is situational and hard to cast at 6 mana without the trap condition) or Acorn Catapult (a weak artifact) would have been better. Karador at 8 CMC is very expensive but has built-in cost reduction and can be cast from graveyard-style effects. Cobra Trap is extremely situational and unlikely to be cast for its trap cost, making it arguably the better discard.
annotations.actionTaken: Discarded Karador, Ghost Chieftain to hand size
annotations.betterLine: Discard Cobra Trap instead — it's a 6-mana situational card that rarely gets its trap cost enabled, while Karador has significant cost reduction potential and graveyard synergy with Teneb, the Harvester

annotations.description: Playing Myriad Landscape instead of an untapped basic land means Gem25F Analyst has less mana available this turn and next turn (since Myriad Landscape enters tapped). With 5 lands on board (3 untapped after this play), they have no meaningful plays this turn anyway with their hand of expensive spells. However, playing an untapped basic (Island or Swamp) would give them 4 available mana, which still isn't enough for their spells but keeps them more flexible for holding up Soul Manipulation (1UB = 3 mana, which they could do with either land drop). With Myriad Landscape entering tapped, they only have 3 available mana sources (2 Islands + 1 Swamp), which is exactly enough for Soul Manipulation. But playing Island would give them 3 Islands + 1 Swamp = 4 mana, still enough for Soul Manipulation with mana to spare. The Myriad Landscape is better played later when you can sacrifice it immediately or when the tempo loss matters less. Playing Island now keeps the option to play Myriad Landscape later while having more mana available. That said, the ramp from Myriad Landscape is valuable long-term, and playing it early maximizes the chance of having mana to activate it. This is close but slightly suboptimal sequencing.
annotations.actionTaken: Played Myriad Landscape (enters tapped) as land drop for the turn

However, looking more carefully, Soul Manipulation has two modes: counter a creature spell AND/OR return a creature card from graveyard to hand. But wait - why did they cast Soul Manipulation in the first place if neither mode is beneficial? They're countering nothing useful and have no creatures in graveyard. If they must choose at least 1 mode, and the only viable mode is countering their own creature (bad), then Cancel might be correct to avoid that. But the real blunder may have been casting Soul Manipulation in the first place with no good targets. However, we're only evaluating this specific decision. annotations.description: Gem25F Analyst played a land before casting Merfolk Windrobber. With Military Intelligence on the battlefield, deploying creatures before combat is important to enable attacking with two creatures to trigger the card draw. However, the more significant issue is sequencing: playing the land first is fine, but they should also cast Merfolk Windrobber in this main phase to have it ready for combat. The real concern is whether they cast the Windrobber at all this turn. Additionally, with Blackblade Reforged on the battlefield and now 6 lands (after playing the Swamp), the equipment could be relevant. The land play itself is correct - making the land drop is important. But casting Merfolk Windrobber before combat would be ideal since it has flying and could deal combat damage to trigger milling, and if they have another creature, Military Intelligence would trigger. Looking at the board, Gem25F Analyst has no creatures on the battlefield, so casting Windrobber pre-combat is correct to at least start building a board presence. This is just a land drop though - they likely plan to cast Windrobber next. This seems like a reasonable sequencing choice (land before spell).
annotations.actionTaken: Played Swamp from hand
annotations.betterLine: Playing the land first is actually correct sequencing (land before spells to have mana available). This is fine as long as they follow up with Merfolk Windrobber.

annotations.description: Gem25F Analyst spent 7 mana to equip Blackblade Reforged, but looking at their battlefield, they have no creatures to equip it to. The Whirler Rogue ability mention suggests there may be a Whirler Rogue and Thopters on the board (not fully listed), but equipping Blackblade Reforged for 7 mana is an enormous tempo loss when the board state doesn't warrant it. They have 8 lands so Blackblade would give +8/+8, but spending their entire turn on this instead of developing board presence is questionable at best. More critically, the reasoning text cuts off mid-sentence, suggesting the AI didn't finish evaluating options before choosing. With Merfolk Windrobber available as a cheap play that provides evasive damage, mill synergy with Anowon (their commander likely), and card draw potential, casting the Windrobber and keeping mana open would have been far more efficient. Paying 7 mana to equip when they could instead cast a creature and hold up mana is a massive tempo mistake.
annotations.actionTaken: Activated Blackblade Reforged's Equip {7} ability, spending all available mana on equipping.
annotations.betterLine: Cast Merfolk Windrobber for {U}, potentially use Whirler Rogue's tap ability to make a creature unblockable for combat damage and mill triggers, and hold remaining mana open for future plays.

annotations.description: Equipping Blackblade Reforged to the ground-based Whirler Rogue (making it 8/8 without evasion) rather than a Thopter token (making it 7/7 with flying) is suboptimal. A 7/7 flyer is harder to block and deals more reliable damage. Additionally, keeping Whirler Rogue unequipped preserves the option to tap artifacts (including the other Thopter) to make the equipped Thopter unblockable.
annotations.actionTaken: Equipped Blackblade Reforged to Whirler Rogue (2/2 ground creature, becoming 8/8)
annotations.betterLine: Equip Blackblade Reforged to a Thopter token (1/1 flyer, becoming 7/7 flyer) for better evasion and damage potential

annotations.description: By attacking with only Whirler Rogue, Gem25F Analyst missed the Military Intelligence trigger which requires attacking with 2+ creatures. They could have tapped Blackblade Reforged + 1 Thopter token to make Whirler Rogue unblockable, then attacked with Whirler Rogue + the other Thopter token to trigger Military Intelligence and draw a card.
annotations.actionTaken: Attacked with only Whirler Rogue, missing the Military Intelligence trigger.
annotations.betterLine: Tap Blackblade Reforged + 1 Thopter token for Whirler Rogue's unblockable ability, then attack with Whirler Rogue and the remaining Thopter token to trigger Military Intelligence for a free card draw.

annotations.description: Kept Penumbra Spider back for defense when attacking Haiku Gramps who has zero creatures on the battlefield. The 2 extra damage is free since there are no blockers, and the defensive value of holding back a 2/4 reach is marginal when the primary flying threat is just Breena (1/3).
annotations.actionTaken: Held back Penumbra Spider 2/4 as a blocker while attacking with Teneb and Monk Realist
annotations.betterLine: Attack with all three creatures including Penumbra Spider for 2 additional free damage against an empty board

annotations.description: Giving Teneb, the Harvester double strike via Duelist's Heritage is very dangerous because Teneb's combat damage trigger lets Gem3F ESPN pay {2}{B} to reanimate a creature from any graveyard. Double strike means TWO combat damage triggers, potentially allowing ESPN to reanimate two creatures (like Demanding Dragon, Chameleon Colossus, or Karador from the graveyards). This massively benefits ESPN.
annotations.actionTaken: Targeted Teneb, the Harvester with Duelist's Heritage to give it double strike
annotations.betterLine: Either decline to use Duelist's Heritage entirely (it's a 'may' ability), or if politically desirable, target the Monk Realist instead, which has a far less impactful combat damage trigger and doesn't enable double reanimation.

annotations.description: Gem3F ESPN has Acorn Catapult untapped and 1 untapped Forest available to activate it (cost {1}, {T}). They could have used it to ping Haiku Gramps (or any target) before damage, creating a Squirrel token. While the Squirrel goes to the damaged player, pinging Haiku Gramps for 1 extra damage before Teneb's combat damage trigger is pure upside - it adds 1 more damage and Teneb is already getting through unblocked. Alternatively, they could ping one of their own creatures to get the Squirrel token themselves. Declining a free activation with available mana is a missed opportunity.
annotations.actionTaken: Passed priority without activating Acorn Catapult, despite having the mana and the artifact untapped.
annotations.betterLine: Activate Acorn Catapult targeting Haiku Gramps for 1 extra damage (Haiku Gramps gets a Squirrel but takes 1 more damage), or target own Monk Realist to create a Squirrel token for themselves before damage.

annotations.description: Missed activating Acorn Catapult to ping their own creature/self to create a 1/1 Squirrel token. This is free value - the Squirrel token would help with Hour of Reckoning's Convoke cost (in hand) and would survive the board wipe since it destroys nontoken creatures.
annotations.actionTaken: Passed without activating any abilities
annotations.betterLine: Activate Acorn Catapult targeting themselves or their own creature (like Monk Realist) to create a 1/1 Squirrel token, which synergizes with Hour of Reckoning's Convoke and survives the wipe

annotations.description: Gem3F ESPN selected Demanding Dragon as the target for Teneb's reanimation trigger but then couldn't pay the {2}{B} cost because they had already tapped too many lands during their turn, leaving only two lands untapped (needing three mana). The entire selection was wasted - they got nothing from Teneb's combat damage trigger. Even if they had the mana, the choice of target matters: Karador, Ghost Chieftain would have provided recurring value by letting them cast creatures from their graveyard every turn, which is a much stronger long-term engine than a one-shot 5 damage from Demanding Dragon's ETB.
annotations.actionTaken: Selected Demanding Dragon as the reanimation target, then failed to pay the {2}{B} cost, getting nothing from Teneb's trigger.
annotations.betterLine: Should have planned mana usage earlier in the turn to keep {2}{B} available for Teneb's trigger. With proper mana management, they could have reanimated Karador, Ghost Chieftain for long-term graveyard recursion value, or Demanding Dragon for immediate board impact.
